Or, to put it the other way around: it is a conclusion drawn from the realization that the grave has been taken from us, that we no longer have a grave.
Rape and <child abuse>, and so on. But if we subtract all these concrete offenses, what remains as a pure crime of “inhumanity”?
A crime against God—humanity, or the Great <Something>?

What is the structure of the thing that can be protected or attacked by such a crime, when the crime is defined not through a precise description of an act but exclusively through its general hideousness?

The end of the younger Masaryk affects me deeply and completely personally, at that point within private life where the existential contact takes place between the great whole and the individual human being placed at the disposal of the World Spirit.
With Masaryk’s suicide, the European age in which one could choose between West and East comes to an end.
The elder Masaryk had been a true European katechon, a restraining force: the katechon of Western liberal democracy.

With an astonishing degree of historical consciousness—infinitely greater than anything the German politicians, philosophers, or historians of the time could summon—old Masaryk chose the West after the most thorough reflection. He knew Russia and the East better than most Germans, Poles, or Serbs of his time. He loved that Russia. But his intellectual decision was for the West. He married an American woman, and that marriage became a symbol larger than their private lives: the symbol of his choice of the West.

The son born from that marriage, who has now killed himself in Prague, was the guarantor of that Western choice, together with Beneš, whom Masaryk had designated as his successor. And so this age now ends with the son throwing himself from a window of the Czernin Palace. This is more than the earlier Defenestrations of Prague: that of the New Town councillors in 1419, and that of the imperial councillors in May 1618. This is the Czechs’ own suicidal fall from the window, following the fall of the Germans and the many suicides of April 1945.
What wars will this third Defenestration of Prague set in motion?

I feel that this is one of those moments in my life when the personally private and the all-encompassing universal meaning of events coincide, and when God’s ordering shadow touches my small individual life.
I must tell my daughter this so that I have a witness.
Just as Joseph de Maistre’s parents told their child, while he was playing, in 1772:
“Child, a great disaster has occurred. The Pope has dissolved the Jesuit order.”
How do I grasp the depth of this moment?
How long can I manage to remain at this depth?
I quickly read the Grewe–Küster discussion, Nuremberg as a Legal Question, Stuttgart 1947.
I suspect Grewe knows the legal opinion I wrote in the summer of 1945 on the international-law crime of aggressive war and the principle nullum crimen sine lege—no crime without a law.
However unpleasant Küster sometimes seems, and however cautiously Grewe conducts himself, a great deal becomes visible.
Not only questions and arguments that are properly legal.

Something infinitely more important as well. This discussion is evidence that we in Germany are sitting at the very core and center of the modern problem, and that we must work through this entire terrible problem within ourselves and with ourselves, without help from East or West.
We must carry out this whole monstrous “trial” inside ourselves—as an internal German matter and at the same time as a matter concerning the whole world.
Both disputants have the intellectual stature and the beginnings of what would be needed.

We must produce the enemy within ourselves so that we do not stand facing an empty void. Because none of the arguments coming to us from outside can bind or convince us. That becomes tangible precisely in Küster’s style.
But in no essential respect have we been annihilated—not morally, and not legally. We are occupied, but we have not been conquered.
Only someone who knows his booty better than the booty knows itself can truly conquer it. So who in East or West could conquer us?

The military, technical-industrial, and economic giants who hold us on the ground and keep us subjugated do not even want to know us or learn about us. They throw us to the émigrés to be devoured. And the émigrés do not want to know us either. They merely want to prove that the positions they held twenty years ago were right and to collect their compensation.

The tu quoque—“you too”—reveals the murky kind of cleverness characteristic of people like Küster. He continually mixes together the very things that he continually and cleverly claims to distinguish.

Naturally, an inhuman person has no right to reproach another inhuman person for also being inhuman. But we, as observers and judges, certainly may conclude that it would not be justice if someone who himself commits inhuman acts appointed himself judge over another person and sentenced him to death as an inhuman being.
The moment I begin speaking of “inhumanities”—beyond the already recognized offenses of murder, robbery, and rape—I leave the sphere of institutional human law and legal positivism.

I enter the Hobbesian state of nature. And there the tu quoque opens the judicial stage of the bellum omnium contra omnes, the war of everyone against everyone. Then everyone becomes not only everybody else’s potential murderer, but everybody else’s criminal judge as well.
The murderers of one side sit in judgment over the murderers of the other and refuse to hear tu quoque.
Two beautiful confirming quotations come running toward me like messengers:

“Under all circumstances, the unavoidable fate of the legal profession, as a consequence of technical and economic development, is an increasing tendency to regard whatever law happens to be in force as a rational technical apparatus—an apparatus without any sacred content and therefore capable at any time of being rationally redesigned for particular purposes.
This fate can be concealed by the growing tendency, arising for general reasons, to submit to existing law, but it cannot actually be averted.”
Who besides me spoke about this before 1933 and tried to do something about it?
Friedrich Engels, in the posthumously published essay “Force and Economics in the Formation of the German Empire,” written in 1888:
Bismarck had “proved” to the German bourgeoisie “that he knew better than they themselves did what was good for them.” That is my beloved Bruno Bauer quotation of 1849!

Wave and particle, representation and nominalism appear at the same time in intellectual history and apparently belong together in some topological and wave-like sense.
Veritas in verbo (dicto), non in re.
Truth lies in the word—in what is said—not in the thing itself.
Nominalism: not presence, but making something present within consciousness—something absent, or better, something that is not actually there.
Dictatorship and nominalism: the dictamen, the command or authoritative pronouncement.
Veritas in dictamine, non in re.
Truth lies in the command, not in the thing.

The re- in representare seems to contain an overcompensating urge to intensify, an urge that accompanies the feeling that something is not real. It does not simply mean “back.” But perhaps it originally connects with tendencies toward restoration.

Sociology from the standpoint of the dispossessed: the antechamber takes possession of the salon; the caretaker takes possession of the villa; the former inmates of the prisons become the new rulers; the enemies win and now appear as victims, demanding compensation and bonuses for martyrdom.
The reverse would be sociology from the standpoint of those who have arrived. But the successful rarely practice sociology.

From Germany’s point of view, the Second World War was not merely a war on two fronts. It was also a war combining two <different> kinds of war.

H. tried to wage two different wars—and it was clumsy beyond belief to imagine this could work: a nondiscriminating war against the West; and a discriminating war against Russia and the Slavic peoples. For that reason, the true answer came from the East, from Russia.
The master of the Nuremberg Trial was the Soviet Union, which made use of American moral outrage.

Russia’s role in the Nuremberg Trial—I mean only the great main trial before the International Military Tribunal, which was intended as the fundamental trial—became clearly visible in the way the Katyn case was handled, in Rudenko’s shot at Hermann Göring, and at various other moments in the proceedings.
The only real question is whether Germany belongs to the Russian or the American Großraum, the greater sphere of intervention.
